Overview

About the atlas

The atlas brings together reports of border closures and restrictions between 21 October 2016 and 21 October 2026. Each record is an entry compiled from those reports about a restriction and its changes over time. The atlas documents historical evidence; it does not provide live information about whether a border is open.

What does the dataset cover?

The main dataset covers restrictions at land borders and international river ferries, including restrictions on particular travellers or goods. An entry may concern one crossing, several crossings or a wider border policy. Related entries can describe parts of the same event.

Routine opening hours, individual visa refusals and checks that allow passage are excluded. Selected COVID-19 rules on international passenger travel in Australia, New Zealand and the UK are shown as green country outlines for context and kept out of the land-border charts. Read their sources ↗

How should I read the map?

The reason given for a restriction is indicated by its colour; the Map key explains the colours and symbols. Small dots mark named crossings. Their size does not show duration, severity or the number of records.

Lines represent broader restrictions, such as a border-wide rule or a rule affecting several crossings whose precise extent is not established. A solid line means the source explicitly describes a border-wide rule; a dotted line means its geographical extent is limited or uncertain. The line does not, by itself, establish that every crossing along it was closed. Locations are matched to each dated phase, so an entry can change from a line to a point as its scope changes.

Grey border references can be selected to find associated entries, including those awaiting a checked crossing location. Earlier crossing records can also be displayed using the optional toggle under Search & zoom → Filters → Map detail & other records. These references do not establish whether a border was open or closed in the selected month.

Read the location review and sources ↗

What do the dates mean?

Observed closure uses reports of passage actually being stopped or restricted. Policy in force uses the recorded dates when an official restriction applied; these may differ from when movement stopped or resumed on the ground.

Announced closure dates come from a planned schedule, which may not have been carried out. Repeated closures describes a period with interruptions and possible openings, rather than one continuous closure.

Reports often omit a precise start or reopening date. A record can appear in a month without covering every day of it. A last report of closure is not treated as a reopening, and an unknown end is not extended to the present.

Other kinds of date evidence

These groups overlap: one record can contain several kinds of timing evidence. A missing reopening date does not mean a closure continued.

How are the rationales grouped?

The categories, labelled “coded rationale” in the records, summarise reasons given in the sources. Assigning them requires judgement: a closure may have several stated rationales, and reports are not always clear. The categories are nonexclusive.

An official rationale is an authority’s stated explanation. A reported explanation and an analytical interpretation are different kinds of evidence; each assignment retains its attribution and qualifications.

Grey means no category has been assigned. This can reflect missing evidence or a documented reason outside the categories.

How rationale coding works

A closure imposed to prevent disease belongs under Health and biosecurity; a blockade protesting health restrictions belongs under Policy and socioeconomic demands. Health and biosecurity separates human disease from animal and plant disease.

Interstate disputes and pressure, Power and regime politics, and Policy and socioeconomic demands distinguish different political mechanisms. Several codes do not imply that every rationale applied throughout the record.

Browse the records and their coding →

Coverage varies by place, time and available sources. The charts describe the collected records; they do not measure how often closures happen worldwide.

How do I find and download records?

Use Search & zoom to choose a continent or search across all recorded dates. Select a border, marker or list entry to read its dates and source links. Read all records opens a wider reading view.

Click the date above the timeline to choose a month and year directly. Play timeline moves through the months; the speed control offers 1×, 2×, 4× and 8× playback.

The Dataset tab provides a searchable browser view and the complete Excel workbook. Download CSV saves matching entries as a spreadsheet. Save view saves an image of the map and its key.

How can I check the sources?

Each record links to its sources and explains any uncertainty. A later review may establish a more precise date, clarify who or what was affected, revise the reason assigned to a restriction, or show that an earlier claim is unsupported. The current entry reflects the latest assessment; earlier findings remain in the review history so the changes can be traced.

Some sources were available in full; others only as extracts. Different websites can repeat the same original report, so the number of links is not a count of independent confirmations.

How to cite

Lamarque, H. (2026) Global Border Closures Atlas. Available at: https://lamarque-mapping.github.io/Border-Closure-Atlas/ (Accessed: 24 October 2026).

When discussing a particular release, also give the dataset date shown above.
